new_statements.quote: Oceanic languages in this region typically have smallish phonemic inventories, with no complex articulations except prenasalized stops, and with stress being predictable. Bilua conforms exactly to this. Touo adds to this basic system the interesting distinction between breathy and normal voice in initial syllables, and a sixth vowel, /ɔ/. There is only a marginal voicing distinction among stop consonants. Stress is predictable. [Table 3, p. 333, row 'predictable stress': BILUA 'yes', TOUO 'yes?', LAVUKALEVE 'largely', SAVOSAVO 'largely']

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress in Touo is described as predictable (non-contrastive), i.e. rule-governed like the surrounding Oceanic languages, but the source never says which syllable carries it; the summary table hedges the claim with a question mark. No placement rule can be extracted.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated for Touo (the hedge 'yes?' in Table 3 is the only qualification).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level, in a comparative section on phonological inventories; the Touo facts rest on Terrill & Dunn's unpublished field notes (p. 314), so this is first-hand but summary-level. No citation forms or examples given.
new_statements.identity_note: Touo is the speakers' own name; the literature calls it Baniata/Mbaniata (a village name) and Tryon & Hackman 1983 list two Rendova wordlists, Mbaniata (no. 20) and Lokuru (no. 21), distinguished by an r/l correspondence; Terrill 2011 treats one language, Touo (touo1238), with no dialect specified.

sources.citation: Todd, Evelyn M. 1975. The Solomon language family. In S. A. Wurm (ed.), New Guinea area languages and language study, Vol. 1: Papuan languages and the New Guinea linguistic scene, 805-846. Pacific Linguistics C-38.
sources.note: Sec. 2.13.2.2 Phonology and orthography (pp. 808-809) gives only the Savosavo phoneme table and says the other three languages' phonology 'has not been studied in depth'; the only stress remark concerns Savosavo (no automatic stress rule formulated). Nothing on Baniata stress; notes Baniata vowel length marked by informant and occasional nasalization.
